segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We going to talk for a little while. I tell them all the time, we're going to talk about what's written on here. That is what I will ask you. The reason they're doing this is if the students listen to this, they might learn something from us full Cherokees. Some of these students are just learning Cherokee, that's the purpose of this. What's your first name in English and Cherokee?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: They call me Dorothy Lee Ice. I don't use my middle name, they forget to write it down.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What's your Cherokee name?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Tsugatli.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Tsugatli.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I haven't been able to find anybody to tell me the meaning in English.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Tsugatli, who gave you that name?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: My granny, when I was little. When someone would come, I would run and get everybody water. Or whatever was on the table, like candy or kanatchi, all of that. They would say, what a giving girl, they would say. I wasn’t talking good yet, but I could walk good. What a giving girl. When they all left, my granny talked loud. She would say, “Get Tsugatli. Let's go draw some water.” She had two chilli cans with strips, I carried those two. Herself, she carried the bigger one, I don't know what size, 10 or 20. I used to help them out, without them telling me to. I liked carrying water and getting it. It was deep. There were two holes. I don't know if the water ate the ground out. It was about that deep [gesture] and you would dip in there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Boy.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I really liked to help out. She would say, “Go check on your mom, see what she wants.” I think I was probably in the way. That's why she was sending me away. They would never tell me to move. They would just have me do errands so I would leave.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I wish kids were like that these days.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They call tsukatlesgi would be hospitable.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I never could find it, but I wanted to learn what it was.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Hospitable.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I'm 87 years old and I haven't learned it yet.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You're that age? You don't look that old.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Thank you.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You're getting around good.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: When I go to the stomp grounds, I put the shell shakers on. I know that really helps me out.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, I'll be, where were you born and what year?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Cedar Tree.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, just over there.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Toward Briggs on the east side. I grew up at Cedar Tree. And that big, long building out there, I helped there, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really? Well, I'll be.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Would you say Pine Tree in English?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: No, Cedar.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Cedar Tree.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Briggs Cedar Tree.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They call it the Assembly Grounds. What year were you born?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: In thirty-five, December 26, ‘35.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You were born close to Christmas.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: At one o'clock, midnight.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Were you born there?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: In the woods.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: In the woods, yeah.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: In a one-room house.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really. If you see it now, it seems like a small house. Don't it? At that time, it seemed like a big house.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Mom had all of her things in there. My dad built it with one room. He cut down the wood.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really? By himself? Well, I'll be. Where did you just grow up, there?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Just there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You grew up there?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I also hunted crawdads there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Gah-lee.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: A few of us kids, while our mothers were washing the clothes. There were two creeks and one was really cold. The other wasn't where they did the washing. They would be scrubbing, and we would be hauling the water crawling on the rocks.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was it like when you were growing up? Were there a lot of houses close to where you were born?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: There were a lot of houses that they built themselves. My late grandpa had wood this size [gesture] that he split in half and used that to build a two-room house. That's where my grandpa and grandma lived.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, I'll be, yeah.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: And my dad, he built a one-room house with the bigger logs. My mom had everything in there. She had two beds, a thin stove, a dresser, and a place to hang clothes. A cook stove was in the corner, and Dad made a long dining table.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Man, I remember a long time ago, the cooking area was dirt.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: It was outside. Granny and my grandpa had it like that. If he killed a pig, he would make the grease in there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How many siblings did you have?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Five.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So there were five of you.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Three boys and two of us girls. I'm the oldest.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You're the oldest? Are some of them still alive?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: One, no, two boys are alive.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You and your siblings, for instance, would they tell you to go outside when they're talking? They used to do that a long time ago when the elders were talking. They would tell us to go outside. When they would tell you that, what did you all find to play with?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: We would crawl on the trees, or where they had cut wood, we would jump on that. That was dangerous if it rolled. When I think about that now, it scares me. We were doing dangerous stuff. The tops of the trees that were broken, we would run and jump over them. We were doing dangerous stuff. We didn't make our own toys, like you were talking about. I guess my dad found a box somewhere, I think it was a baby stroller. It had wheels. He went by a junkyard and brought the wheels. I took them off and I flipped a box over. He had some big nails. I guess they were for building. I don't know what they were for. To me, they were really long. The bar was laying around, but I didn't know where he got it. I cleaned it and put the wheels on and put it back. I got the big nails, bent them, and put them in. We would ride it when the kids would come. There was a ridge close to the house. We would push. Somebody would get back on it or stand on it. It was funny, I think about it and laugh to myself. We were doing dangerous stuff. Also, when we found a car fender on the road, we would pull. When there was snow and ice, we would put it up on a high ridge. Someone would sit on it with a rope and pretend to make the turns, but it wasn't turning. And somebody would be standing on this side [gesture]. It was dangerous, but it was funny at that time.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I did the same thing growing up.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: It was funny, I want to tell somebody. They would say it's too stupid, it's too stupid. I was having a good time. I didn't have nothing bought to play with. When we would play horse, we would use the old milk boxes they bought at the store. We would stomp on them, and they would fold onto our shoes. We did anything to the others, they were the horses. They sounded good, too, like a horse was coming on that rug. I could talk a lot, I know I was pretty small. I don't want to forget it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is it different now from where you grew up?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: It's different, the kids will be listening when adults are talking. Even when they're running them off, they won’t move. They will not mind. When they're talking Cherokee, they're doing the same thing, but they don't understand it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, what you were just talking about, you go back and think about all of that.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: All the time. I live by myself and have two dogs in the house. I call them Chihuahuas, but they're not full. And two are outside. They came by themselves. They dump them out by the mailbox. The kids that play there have a big turnaround area to play in that put rocks there. It's fixed really good. That's where the stray dogs play.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really. I think about when I was growing up, too. How it was back then and how things have changed. I guess the same thing comes back to you?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I'm always thinking about that. I think when somebody comes, I'm going to tell them what little I know. They need to know what happened a long time ago. The kids need to know. The kids will say, “That's too stupid” and go out.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Do you have somebody to talk Cherokee to every day?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: If they're a speaker, we talk all in Cherokee. If not, either one.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: It's important to have someone to talk Cherokee to daily.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: It’s good. I'm thankful when someone is talking Cherokee, I'm thankful.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Are your siblings still alive so you all can talk to each other?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: If you can go in the woods, they all live on the hill. They're fluent speakers.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: It's important to talk Cherokee.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I'm extremely thankful. We're going to forget it. When us speakers are gone, it's going to be all English or Spanish. Also, at the stomp grounds, I was pretty small when I started shaking the shells there. I had little bitty ones that my grandma made. That's what I grew up doing at Chewey and toward Vian. I grew up wearing those.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Being involved?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: But I didn't know how to tie them, just in a little bit somebody had to fix them. It was a long way.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: You were talking about Tsu. When did they stop that at Tsu?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Tsu, I think they are still having it, I forgot what night they dance. It's east of that store, I don't know how many times they moved. Across the road from the highway, it's right next to the road. I don't know how many times they have moved. I went by there last summer. They still have the dust. I don't know how they move it. I myself don't know.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: When's the last time they danced over there?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I think they said they were dancing just a while ago. They were just talking about it. I've never been there.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: It's been a long time since I've been there.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I remember when I was a kid, they would get together with Vian there. The was a crippled old man at Tsu. Oh, I'm thinking of a different place, Mulberry Hollow.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Kuwah.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Kuwah, yeah, we used to help the old man cut wood. I remember his wife was a great cook. Gah-lee, we would eat like it was Thanksgiving or Christmas. Gah-lee, I remember that old lady’s cooking. I forgot that old lady’s name. I do know that old man’s name was Raymond Chewey. He was crippled and a medicine man, too. But he couldn't walk good. I remember we were helping him cut wood. Yeah, that's what we were always doing.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: That’s right. I was doing that at Cedar Tree. I helped my uncle cut wood. Now I think about it, I was probably in the way. I was crawling on the trees while they were cutting wood. When I think about it, I was probably in the way. But I was helping them with the wood.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: But you were helping them.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I would grab the ends that were cut off. I would stack them on the side, that's what I was doing. I was never still, I'm still like that. I never have any progress. I'll still be doing the same thing. Wood will be piled up. I just move it around, but it looks different. That's true.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s like that when you get old. It seems like you've done a lot, but when you look around, you haven't done nothing. Where did you work?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: When I was growing up, I picked strawberries and planted them. I kept the seeds in my apron. I had a broom that I had broken off, and that's what I used. The road going towards Stilwell used to be a strawberry patch, but now it's full of poke salad. I would make a hole and step on it. I planted a lot of it. I wasn't even 12 yet, I was always working. I guess I was working. I don't know, when I think about it. When I finished that, I would draw water and start running. I think I just wanted to run around. I would fill everything up for Mom. When I was done, Mom would tell me to go play. I would think of something else, like her wood cook stove, to get her wood for that.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What about as an adult?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: The same way, I'm never still. I'm sitting here with my mouth moving. I love people and children. I was six years old when I started going to the stomp grounds. Wearing shell shakers that my grandma made. When she was still and resting, she would make those. Vian – I don't remember what they called it, the stomp grounds at Chewey. It was on this side [gesture] to the south of the road. There was a creek there and the water was flowing really good. They had their fire there, they had moved a few times. As of now, it was east of the store. It's also moved a few times.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you ever learn how to play the guitar? What do they call that in Cherokee? Diqwanvgisdi or what do you all call them?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: That's all I've heard - diqwanvgisdi.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: diqwanvgisdi - guitar.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I grew up playing, I would help my dad. He was a fiddler. But the only keys I was using were A and D. And himself a fiddle. I grew up dancing on a stage at Westville. There weren't enough women with dresses dancing, but there were a lot of men or boys. We weren't adults. My dad played music there a long time ago.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What they called square dance.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Yeah, that. Mom would save four 25-pound flour bags. When she would get four, she would sew them together, lay it on the bed, hemmed it, made a circle, put a hole in the middle, cut it, and hemmed it. Those were my dresses, I always had on a new dress. It was just a flour sack but it was new.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Right, that's what they used to do a long time ago. Like you're saying, the men would make shoes out of flour sacks. They would be walking around wearing those shoes in the snow. They also wore the bread sacks, too.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I didn't have good shoes. I would do that when I had to go out.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And then, like you're saying, they would use the bread sacks and go hunting for rabbits, yeah.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I used to hunt, too, when I was 12 years old. I was coming a long way down through a big thicket. When my mom wanted rabbits or squirrels, I would go down the hill. I had pockets on the inside to put the squirrels, but I didn't put the rabbits in there. That's what I would do. She would want about six of them to make dumplings. I would go a long way, I think it was called Copeland Bottoms for a little while, and I would go back.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: How were you killing them?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Carrying them around? In my coat pocket.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: The squirrels and rabbits, how were you killing them? Were you shooting them?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: There were a lot of them. They weren't wild. The rabbits weren't either. They moved slow in the snow. I was good with a .22. Not now, but I still have it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: I bet you're still accurate.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I used to be.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What about now?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I don't know. I can't even eat rabbit now, I see them. I can't eat a chicken either, I gave it up a long time ago. But I'll buy it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What about now, do you sew or make things? Do you do stuff like that?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: What I do now for money, I sew white cloths. I have it scattered and covered up in a big area. I sew the white cloths and sell them. Just if they ask for them. You have to use a lot of thread, so they bring their own thread. I wish I would've bought it. If I was told what I was going to be doing, I would've bought it. The Cherokee store can't afford to buy them. It's five dollars a roll. It's really good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What were your parents’ names?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: My mom’s name was Bark, and my dad was Dreadfulwater. Dianna Bark and Robert were her parents. When it comes to my grandma, she would tell me I didn't need to know, is what she would say. She wouldn't tell you. She wouldn't even tell us where she was born, came from or grew up. She would get on to us. Galilo and Tsan Ganisini. That's as far as it went on that side.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where I'm from there are a lot of Barks.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: He grew up around Vian, Marble City, and Chewey. He left from there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about your dad and mom? What were their parents’ names, do you know?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: My mom’s mother’s name was Dianna Holt and Robert Bark. I don't know on my dad’s side. He wouldn't tell you. He would be walking and say, “You don't need to know,” and get on to us. But he wouldn't hit us. But on my mom’s side, she would say, “if I knew, I would tell you.” I guess she didn't know, or she didn't want to tell us.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess she thought you didn't need to know.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: That's all I know, but I wanted to learn. I would think at least I would know. I just know what I told you all.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If your parents were still alive, what would you want to ask them?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I guess they told me everything. They were always saying, “You need to know this.” There were five of us, but I was ahead of them. I was seven when my sister was born. I also fixed cars. When I was 12, I would overhaul them. I would take everything off myself. I used a chain and hoist to pull the block, put it on the shelf, and clean it all up. I don't know if that's necessary nowadays. I would clean all the oil and put everything back together. At two o'clock, my dad would drive it. It was funny, I was running all over the place, I never walked. I don't know why. Now I barely walk, my knees are weak. I guess it's supposed to be that way. I'm 87 years old. Cars break down, too, is what I think.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We get old just like the cars. Yeah. You did and saw a lot of things in your life that they don't do now. They stopped a long time ago. Like you were saying, the way you grew up, if you look around and see others, they don't do that anymore. Like the things we used to do, they don't do anymore these days.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: No, kids don't play anymore. That creek in town by the bluff is where I ran around. When I wanted water, I would lay down and think that's what horses do, making a sound when I drink.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What about when families got together to eat, sing or do things a long time ago? Do you still do that?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: They would do that at any time. The women would cook chicken and dumplings in a big pot. All of them would fry chicken and bake cornbread and clabber milk. It was so good. They were eating real good.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Do you all still do that?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: The men would play cards or dominoes. We didn't mess with that. We made our own stuff to play with and named things.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Also a long time ago they would play bingo.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Yes, they would do that outside. For instance, they would hang out the old gas lanterns. They would play that there.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They would throw rubbers, too.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I have the rubbers, but I don't have the board. The kids tore it up. But they're easy to make. Just cut the wire, make circles, and hook them on. I have new rubbers. I bought them at a yard sale. I paid 50 cents for them. I wondered how much she was going to say. I don't think she knew what they were. I look at them sometimes, and I think, “This is what you're supposed to do.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You were talking about the clabbered milk, I bet it's hard to find these days.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: No, they put something in there so it won't sour, when you sour it yourself it doesn't do very good. I think the moon has something to do with it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We used to drink that when I was growing – clabbered milk.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Clabbered milk, you don't have to mix it really hard, just softly, and put it on a biscuit. It's really good. I'm hungry now. Not really, you could talk about a lot of things and not stop.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really. There's a lot of things that we did they don't hardly do these days.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Nobody is doing that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Another thing, too, when we used to get together or if somebody was sick, everybody would come. They called it gadvga.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Not now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They don't do that.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: The women would wash the clothes and the kids would draw the water so they could wash the clothes. And the men would cut the wood to cook with or to heat with for the winter. I've participated in everything they were doing. I don't know if I was being nosy, in the way, or what. But if I was close by, they would ask me to go get things like tools, and I would bring it to them. A lot of people from Chewey came. Dad was the only one who had a chain hoist. Just a real chain, the kind that you pull, not the one that was like this [gesture]. I don't know what happened to it. I think the kids sold it. We lived close to someone who bought that stuff and took it somewhere. I don't know where he took it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They probably didn't pay much for it.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: True.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Some of the young kids don't think the things we used are important.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: It's not.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It's just in the way, let's sell it.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: True.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like you were saying, they didn't tell you much about things. For instance, when the Cherokees came from old Cherokee, did anybody tell you what happened when they were coming through?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: My granny would be the only one. I guess her parents knew, but they would tell us we didn't need to know. She wouldn't tell us nothing. I think it was really bad.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That's what they used to say, it was really bad.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: She wouldn't tell you. She would say you don't need to know in a rough way.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What we are now, it's because of the suffering they went through. We have it good now.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Right now, I couldn't use the bought oil. It had to be the pig lard. Then I could eat, or with no grease. To this day, I'm enemies with that oil. But sometimes I have to eat it, if I can't find lard. I eat that salt meat, about that big [gesture]. I melt that, make grease, and save it. I really take care of it. I think I'm used to the way I grew up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You were talking about your parents. Did they plant a garden such as tomatoes, or how do they say it in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Damatli. Damatli, beans, cucumber.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Cucumbers and onions.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: They call them standing, and some people call them long ones.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess that's what your parents planted.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: My mom planted a little, just enough for us to use. But my granny had a big garden. They had working horses to plow with. We didn't have any animals. But I had dogs that I picked up from the road. I still have two that I picked up. I care about them and feel sorry for them because they dump them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: These two I have are big now. They're that tall and heavy. But they're real friendly. I picked those up, too. When you feed them good, then somebody starts wanting them. I tell them to take them. I live too close to the road. It's not that I don’t want them around. I care about them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really, when a dog knows you love them they will love you back. I guess they understand that you're good to them.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: They understand it. You need to talk good to them, and cats, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, and my wife, she talks good to the flowers.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: That's so they understand.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They grow real pretty. She tells me you're supposed to talk to them real nice.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: They will understand.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, they will understand, and they bloom into pretty flowers. She treats the flowers better than me.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Sometimes you feel like that.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: My uncle, my grandpa’s brother, that would be my uncle. There would be small creeks in the woods with rocks around them, real pretty, clear, cold water. He said... we would be sitting by the water, he would say, “Boy...” That reminded me of what you all were talking about. He told me, “One of these days, you will be buying water.” I didn't believe him. I thought that was a big deal. Now I have water in the house, and I'm paying for it, things like that. I also grew up without running water.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Me too.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: And that changed. It was OK.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Plus the bottles of water, that cost money.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: My grandpa, me and my mom lived with my grandpa. He would go by with a light late at night. You could see his light when he was using the bathroom. That’s true what they were telling us what was to come. Right? And it's happened, that's what I'm saying. How did he know? When he told me that I would be buying water some day? He knew what was going to happen. I don't know how he knew, but he did.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Also, this one person said a long time ago, when light bread was a quarter, “Someday, you're going to be paying two dollars.” Now it's over two dollars.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: And some is three dollars.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, gah-lee. Really it's changed a lot.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: A long ways it has changed.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And nowadays, when you buy canned goods such as beans and different things, it's not the same. They add too much things to it. And chicken, too.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: True, I think they put something in it to make you hungry is what I think. You get hungry again for store canned goods. You get full after you eat for a little while. When you get up you're hungry again. I don't know for what. Last night, I opened cans of beans, and they weren’t any good. I've had them for a long time. They were flattened on the bottom. I opened them, what was around a long time ago, pork and beans, that's what they were. I almost went and got Uskani to tell him I found four beans, but I forgot. I started doing something else. It's really changed a hundred percent, as they say were there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: A long time ago, the elders used to put beeswax in their mouths. What did they call it?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Red Seal or Garrett.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, or Garrett.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I tried it, but it made me dizzy. I wasn't stealing it. She had it on the side of the dresser. The lid was softly on there in a glass. There was a bird on it. I think it was Red Seal. She was walking around, and I guess she was watching it. She had a little pretty spoon sitting next to it. I took a little bit and did like that [gesture]. It wasn't even five minutes, I started seeing yellow and red. I went outside and laid down and threw up. That's the only time I know.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It did the same to me, I think it was called Redman. I was buying it secretly and putting in my mouth when my mom couldn't see me. I hid the tobacco underneath. One time my granny came to visit. She saw me putting it in my mouth. One day my mom came in and asked if I was hiding anything in here. I said no, and she asked what that was under the bed. She told me to get it, so I went and got the tobacco. And granny was standing behind. Mom told me to give it to her. My granny was just wanting it. She used up her own tobacco. She turned around laughing. They did me wrong.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: It will make you dizzy real quick, real fast.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: My granny was always using tobacco, that's what the elders used to do a long time ago. They would put that in their mouth. What about these days they say the word tsalegi is written down. What does that mean, atsalegi?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: That's what I asked them, there's a reason they call us tsalegi. What tsalegi is, nobody knows.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: What I've heard, the first white man came and they asked, Who are those people over there? Says tsalegi. You can say in Creek, tsalagi – that's where it came from, they say.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Thats makes sense doesn't it?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: For Creeks tsalagi, what did they say? How would you say that when they live in caves? They say the Cherokees came out of a hole.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I've heard that.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: They told that in the creation story. The Choctaw, Creek, and Chickasaw were saying a Cherokee came out of the hole first, then the Choctaw, Creek, and Seminole came later out of the hole. It was like somebody was being born, like a baby calf or a baby wolf that was wet and dried off and stood up, and another one came out, I don't know what order.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I was going to ask you that. If you think about it, the first one to come out would be the head.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah, I wonder why they were the only one in the creation story, they didn't talk about the other Indians. Why? That's interesting, yeah, that's the creation story.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: My grandma knew a lot of things, but if you asked her anything she would use her apron and tell us we don't know nothing, you don't need to know anything. She would turn around, that's why I don't know anything. And my other granny would make a fist and say you don't need to know.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They were keeping secrets.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I guess they thought it was sad, but I wanted to learn about it. It would be good to know about what happened. I feel like there was a reason, I don't know.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: This one telling jokes was telling a story that he made up about building houses. He burnt one for the blacks to stay in, then another one was whitish for the whites to stay in, and the last one he didn't know what to do with. He went like that [gesture], and after a while, a Cherokee came out.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I've heard something like that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He was just joking.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I've heard stuff like that when they were talking. I would crawl around wanting to hear things like that. But they would slap you in the head. I had a car my dad made with wood. The wheels were made out of wire. I would be playing with and listening but there was no use. Still, these days I want to, and we're not finished learning and hearing about stuff.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: As we're getting old, there's still a lot of things we can learn.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: There's still a lot we can learn.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That's what I tell them.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: If there's something to learn. If not, you won’t be able to.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You can say, if we're all going to learn anything, maybe the ones behind us will learn more. As we're not learning.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Or not pay attention.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah that's it, but us that are here, we don't know what's coming.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: We don't.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We were talking about when you were growing up a little while ago. For instance, you were saying they didn't hardly tell you anything. Some people talk about little people. You know, you've heard about little people, and at night there's different things you can see. Did they tell you things like that?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: No, I've just seen it myself. I don't know if I can tell it or keep it in my mouth, I don't know.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: But really, some people tell some interesting stories about night activity and getting visits. Sometimes they see scary things. Did they ever tell you things like that?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: No, I've heard them talking about things like that, and that white horse. I haven't seen it. The one with the cape riding on a white horse, nothing like that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And some talk about what they call skili. Did they tell you about seeing anything?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: No, they didn't tell me anything, but I believe the elders is what I say or think. I believe they're the ones that are coming around. I believe the people are just sleeping or being still, I believe their minds are still alive. You can see them if it's meant to be.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really some of them, my grandma used to tell me, when there was a noise in the night, she would say, “There's a skili!” and we get scared. She would say sometimes, “The house is shaking!”

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: That I know. Cherokee Nation was telling me they were going to give me a house. I'm not home, no I'm staying at my daughter’s house. They told me, “We're bringing you the house. When you get back, it will be there.” I don't know where I was at, I think I was in town. So I hurried and got home. “We're going to pick a spot to put it.” I thought, “Oh, it wasn't too long!” I went home. When I got home... the little people have a road and they keep to themselves. I don't hear anything and they don't bother me. I set out something on the chair for them to eat. That's what I always did as long as I lived there. Their road was close to the south in my yard. I knew that the road was in my yard but I don't know where it went out or their road is. When...When they brought the house, I thought, “Oh.” They told me they were putting where they wanted it. The second bedroom is on their road. They were always making noise. I don't have anything in there just clothes on a hanger. As far as stuff, I don't have anything. I spend the night in the next room or living room. I've got a cot in there. I really like that. They make noise, and the road is close to the sink. They don’t want to go around.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I have metal lids not glass they make noise with those. I leave out food like cookies, I don't know what they like. I think the dogs see them, too. Their eyes would be moving, then they start barking softly.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: My granny used to do that, too. She would set food out before we went to bed. One time I asked her why she was doing that. She said she was feeding them, but she didn't say what, just giving them something to eat. I woke up in the middle of the night and I could hear the plates.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Yeah, it's like that. Not always, not a long time just long enough to hear the metal lids. And I put my cups up or they'll break them, that’s it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: One time we went to town Saturday afternoon. There was an elder who lived about a mile away who had horses. He brought those, thinking he and Guy would ride them. He said as he was opening the gate, he could hear rocks. I didn't think nothing of it. But the rocks kept coming, then there were big ones. Boy, it scared me and I turned around. And my grandma said, “That's what watches our house.” It really came true and the elder was telling me it really scared him. I came back pretty fast. I guess what you were saying is true, they watch us is what I thought.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Another thing, one time me and my friends were drinking around. It was night, and they said, “Now let's go fishing.” We took a boat and a gig. They told me and my friend, “Just build a fire here. We're going to go gigging for the fish. We'll bring them back and we'll eat good.” We built a fire, and while we were talking, after a little while our friends came running up. They said, “Let's hook the boat up and get out of here.” As we were coming back, they were talking about while they were gigging, after a while rocks were landing in the water. We kept going in the other way. It was getting worse. We thought, “There's something here!” so we ran off.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: At some point, when we were talking about stuff, we started talking about that. There was an older guy there started laughing. He said it wasn't nothing – it was a beaver.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Woya, doya.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Doya, he said. They have tails that wide.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They make a loud noise.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, they are loud.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: It sounds like throwing big rocks. Using its tail, it was doing that because it was getting irritated.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We thought it was a skili or something. We were laughing about it. Where do you go to church when you go to church?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I go to the stomp grounds.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Stomp grounds? I guess Cherokee is included in the singing and preaching.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: It's Cherokee. Some white people, but they use Cherokee, all Cherokee. They have learned it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you know the old songs?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I used to, I haven't been there in a long time. About two years. It makes it rough on me if my truck breaks down. It's old, made in '04. But it runs good, and got new tires on it and a battery. While I'm driving, the body will fall off. I put baling wire on it. I think it's funny. I say that's what we used to do when I was little. I put baling wire with plastic on it. I don't know what to call it. They were big screws, that's what they were made from... I don't know what happened to them. I lost them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like the bobwire on a muffler.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: That's all I have in: wire, pliers, and the cutters. I was at a store, IGA or I guess Savalot. The pliers aren't in there. That's what the kids are doing these days.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Do you know a short song you can sing to us?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: No, I don't know a Cherokee one.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where did you go to school when you were growing up?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Briggs, that's the only place I've been to school to the eighth grade. I started working when I was in the seventh grade, helping people haul water. Then I started driving a Model T and Model A. I also fixed them. Also, for the people close by, they had big 30-gallon buckets made out of wood. I would go to Briggs and get the water. They had a good well and cold water. I put a belt on a bucket, and using my feet, I took out three buckets very quickly. When I would get back, I'd back it up and put them on wheels that were on the barrel. I would put them up. Then I would take the empty ones back to fill up, and then I would take them back to Richard Wilson, Amies, Harrys, and Richards. I would haul water just in a little bit. As for me, I would run around hauling buckets for us to use.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When did you start school?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I just went to school for a little while. I had to work at home. But I finished the eighth grade. My mom taught me how to read and do numbers at home. Like minus and subtract. Then I would write those, and we would lay on the floor. Sometimes we would put our feet on the wall. She had a box, and sometimes we would use black shoe polish to write. It just hangs there, and when I walk by, I would say them. That's all I went to school.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you have a hard time talking English when you started school? My mom taught me that. She would tell me that they were going to ask me this, and you say that.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: In English?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: In English she taught me.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: When you were in school, were there other Cherokees you could talk to?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Yes, there were a lot of my kin folks and a few whites, as far as kids. I don't know, three or six were in the eighth grade, and three of them were white. That's how it was a little.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you ever learn how to write or read in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: My mother taught me before I started school. I knew how really good, and I wrote it for her on paper, and she would write it for me. When I started school, I forgot it. I've started paying attention again. I think I might need to use it again. Someday, it's going to happen. But the white people are learning. They're learning faster than the Cherokees. I forgot it. I shouldn't be forgetting it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: If you don't use it, you forget a little. Same as speaking, you think you won't forget.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: That's what I thought too. I already know it. I don't use it until somebody asks me something. Then I remember it. Some of it, not all of it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about us speaking Cherokee, do you think it's going to fade? For instance, this school – do you think the Cherokee language will continue for many years?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I've been watching what they're learning, and what we learned is different. I think it's going to change. We'll be the same if we’re still alive is what I think. I don't know.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You think the Cherokee language will continue?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: We're not talking good English either, the real Cherokee. The full Cherokee were saying it different, and they're saying it different, too. It's going to end. They're going to forget or we're going to forget it. If I don't use it, I have it on a wall. Sometimes I stop and read it up and down. Some of them I say backwards. I'm saying them different, I'm already forgetting them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So you think it's going to end, Cherokee?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: It's going to fade away and be forgotten is what I think. A different one is going to come is what I think. I don't know.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: The same thing that happened. It's different now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really. I'm glad they're still trying. Cherokee Nation, for instance, these kids going to school, trying to teach them Cherokee so it won’t fade.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: It's fading now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: But we don't know what's coming our way.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I went to Cedar Tree school. I helped the teachers for 15 years. At first, they said to teacher’s aides, “All you have to do is run off papers and get the room ready for her to come in.” Not true! I had been there a week when the teacher left for two weeks. I was by myself then. They didn't even bring me a helper, my boss didn't. What I learned myself is how I started, I thought, “I'm in here alone.” And really, they learned the numbers more and faster to add and subtract. I was telling them, “Subtract, that's take away,” I told them. Then, if it's adding, somebody gave you something then you got more. That's where they understood. They didn't understand the teacher. But they understood my talking. It wasn't the numbers. It was the way I was talking that helped them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes the teachers are higher up teaching.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: That's true, that's it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: This conversation we had, what do you think about Cherokee Nation working on us doing this interview?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I've worked for Cherokee Nation before. It was good back then but they weren't teaching Cherokee then. I was working where they were selling stuff. I was making whites to sell. That's how I was making money, but I wasn't making money. I had to buy yarn and run around looking for something to put grease in. It was just running out.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What about the Cherokee teaching? If you had to say something to help continue that, what would you say?

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: It starts from the heart first before they can learn. Some of them are just playing around. Some of them here are not taking care of it. Some of them, I'm not talking about all of them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Those ones that want to learn.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: It has to start from here [gesture]. You have to pay attention and listen. It starts from here [gesture]. For yourself, if you think you don't need it, you're not going to pay attention. You're going to do it and finish it. I'm like that. I'm not going to give anybody anything. I'm not going to use or scatter it. I don't pay attention.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I don't have anything to do with it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: You're supposed to want to do it. If you want to succeed, you should want to do it.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Yes, that's true.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You're going to try if you really want to learn.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: I want to. My uncle, mother’s brother, his writing is different. But the writing is beautiful. It wasn't like the way my mom learned it. He learned by himself. As for my mom, her mom taught her and two women. The youngest women didn't pay any attention. She said she didn't have anything to do with it. When she grew up, she married a white man. She really didn't use it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well I'm happy we talked.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: Me too, I'm happy. I wanted to talk. I didn't know how long or if it would run out.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There's still room for a lot to talk about, but they allow one hour.

segments.speaker: dorothy-ice
segments.translation: They let me talk for two hours at Briggs. Some of the kids were sliding and saying, “I'm writing, I'm writing!”
